In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

transradial access should not be performed if the operator is not trained and skilled in transradial access, the anatomy of the patient is not amenable to transradial intervention, or the patient’s clinical status is such that transradial intervention would be unsafe.

transradial access should be avoided in the following situations: (1) patients with severe peripheral arterial disease, (2) patients with severe calcified lesions in the radial and brachial arteries, (3) patients with a previous failed transradial attempt, and (4) patients with severe radial artery spasm.

transradial access should be avoided in patients with severe peripheral vascular disease, in patients with small radial arteries, in patients with a history of previous radial artery interventions, and in patients with a radial artery occlusion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
transradial access can be performed in almost any patient.

transradial access should not be used when the patient is not able or willing to cooperate with the procedure, when the patient’s arm is too large for transradial access, when the radial artery is too small or diseased to allow passage of the catheter and sheath, and when the patient has a history of previous radial artery occlusion.5 When Should You Not Use Transradial Access?

transradial intervention is not indicated for patients who are unable to cooperate with the procedure, are not willing to cooperate, are unable to hold their hand still during the procedure, have a hand injury that precludes the use of the radial access site, or have anatomic limitations that prevent access.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most important factor in avoiding complications is to be aware of the potential pitfalls of transradial access.

transradial access should not be attempted in patients with severe vascular occlusive disease.5-7 In addition to this, there are a number of factors that may increase the difficulty of transradial access.

transradial access should not be attempted in patients with severe arterial calcification, small or tortuous vessels, or severe vascular disease.5-7 The most common reasons for failure are radial artery occlusion (RAO) and inability to access the target lesion.8,9 The first obstacle to overcome is RAO.
